meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The true measure of a man is how he treats someone who can do him absolutely no good'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Samuel Johnson. Quote Investigator traces it to Malcolm Forbes (1972) and the Ann Landers columns; the Johnson credit is a modern fabrication.

answer.label: Not Samuel Johnson — a 20th-century saying
answer.authorName: Malcolm Forbes / the Ann Landers columns
answer.authorDates: popularized in the 1970s · not Samuel Johnson (1709–1784)
answer.sourceLine: Samuel Johnson did not write this. The oldest close match — “You can easily judge the character of a man by how he treats those who can do nothing for him” — was credited to publisher Malcolm Forbes in Earl Wilson’s newspaper column in 1972, and this exact “absolutely no good” wording spread through advice columnist Ann Landers and the Chicago Tribune around 1977–1978. Johnson’s name was attached only much later.

source.excerpt: The true measure of a man is how he treats someone who can do him absolutely no good.
trail: The definitive study is Quote Investigator, which traces the earliest close match to publisher Malcolm Forbes via Earl Wilson’s column in 1972 and calls the Johnson (and Goethe) attributions “unsupported by current evidence.”

The scholarly Samuel Johnson site files this line in its Apocrypha, noting there is “no concrete evidence that he ever said it or wrote it” and that it appears in none of his works, letters, or 18th-century biographies.
Per QI, this exact “absolutely no good” phrasing runs through advice columnist Ann Landers (1977–1978) and the Chicago Tribune (1978) — nearly two centuries after Johnson’s death.
source.excerptNote: The exact wording above is documented in the Chicago Tribune (1978), echoing Ann Landers’ columns of 1977–1978; the underlying maxim was credited to Malcolm Forbes in 1972 as “how he treats those who can do nothing for him.”

author.bio: Malcolm Forbes was the flamboyant publisher of Forbes magazine, famous for his epigrams (later collected in The Sayings of Chairman Malcolm, 1978). Quote Investigator’s earliest close match for this “character” maxim credits him in a 1972 newspaper column. The precise “absolutely no good” wording, though, was carried and reshaped by advice columnist Ann Landers later in the 1970s — neither of them Samuel Johnson.

misattribution.heading: How Johnson got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a feel-good character test that reads like classic 18th-century moralism, so it drifted onto the era’s most quotable name. But the paper trail is entirely modern.

items.why: The scholarly Samuel Johnson site places it in its Apocrypha: “no concrete evidence that he ever said it or wrote it” — it is absent from his works, letters, and every 18th-century biography. Quote Investigator likewise calls the Johnson attribution “unsupported by current evidence.”
QI notes the same saying is sometimes pinned on Goethe in 2000s publications with no supporting documentation — another magnet-name attribution.

QI’s earliest close match credits publisher Malcolm Forbes in Earl Wilson’s column (Hartford Courant, 6 Aug 1972): “You can easily judge the character of a man by how he treats those who can do nothing for him.”

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is not Johnson’s: the trail begins in 1972 with Malcolm Forbes and runs through Ann Landers’ columns to the exact “absolutely no good” wording by 1978, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks
lead: The line lands as timeless moral wisdom: real character shows in how you treat people who can neither reward nor punish you. That register — brisk, aphoristic, a little severe — sounds like Dr. Johnson, so his name became the default stamp for an idea he never recorded.

In reality the maxim is a product of 20th-century American print culture: a publisher’s epigram amplified by the enormous readerships of syndicated advice columns, where wordings shift column to column until one crisp version freezes into a ‘quotation’ and picks up a prestigious dead author’s name.
context.pull: An idea Johnson never recorded, wearing his name.
